course.title: Computer Networks — Units 3, 4 & 5
course.description: Interactive, visual and gamified Computer Networks curriculum for NetQuest.
course.contentPolicy: Preserve uploaded course terminology and syllabus scope. Practice and quiz items are authored from those source topics.

modules.title: Network Layer: Design Issues & Services
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of the Network Layer.
Distinguish host-to-host delivery from lower-layer delivery.
Describe connectionless and connection-oriented network services.

lesson.hook: Why does network layer: design issues & services matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Network Layer is Layer 3 of the OSI model and moves packets from a sending host to a receiving host.
Core responsibilities include routing, logical addressing, internetworking and fragmentation.
Network services may be connectionless/datagram based or connection-oriented/virtual-circuit based.
Routers use packet header information and forwarding tables to choose an outgoing interface.

visualization.description: A packet travels across multiple networks and routers instead of only one physical link.

interactiveActivity.description: Animate Host A → Router → Router → Host B; highlight logical address, forwarding table and outgoing interface.

quickCheck.question: Identify which Network Layer function is responsible for selecting the next outgoing interface.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Network Layer: Design Issues & Services.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Network Layer: Design Issues & Services.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Network Layer: Design Issues & Services.

quiz.question: What is the main role of the Network Layer?
options: Move packets from source host to destination host
quiz.explanation: The source material describes host-to-host packet delivery as the main role.

quiz.question: Which device primarily performs Network Layer forwarding?
quiz.explanation: Routers forward packets using network-layer addressing and forwarding tables.

quiz.question: Which service treats each datagram independently?
quiz.explanation: Connectionless service sends datagrams independently.

modules.title: Store-and-Forward Packet Switching
learningObjectives: Trace packet movement through multiple routers.
Relate packet headers to forwarding decisions.

lesson.hook: Why does store-and-forward packet switching matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: A router receives a packet, examines its header, and forwards it through an appropriate output interface.
A forwarding table maps header/address information to outgoing interfaces.
Routing algorithms determine information that is later installed in forwarding tables.
Packets may encounter different paths and delays in a packet-switched network.

visualization.description: Why must a router inspect a packet before forwarding it?

interactiveActivity.description: Interactive packet animation with queues at three routers; click a router to reveal its forwarding-table lookup.

quickCheck.question: Given a forwarding table, select the outgoing interface for a destination prefix.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Store-and-Forward Packet Switching.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Store-and-Forward Packet Switching.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Store-and-Forward Packet Switching.

quiz.question: A forwarding table is used to determine the packet's what?
quiz.explanation: The forwarding table indicates the outgoing interface.

quiz.question: What information does a router examine before forwarding?
quiz.explanation: The router uses header fields to index the forwarding table.

quiz.question: Routing algorithms primarily determine what?
options: Values used to build forwarding information
quiz.explanation: Routing algorithms determine route information used by forwarding.

modules.title: Connectionless vs Connection-Oriented Networks
learningObjectives: Choose an approach for a scenario.

lesson.hook: Why does connectionless vs connection-oriented networks matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Connectionless service treats packets/datagrams independently.
Connection-oriented service establishes, maintains and terminates a logical connection.
Connection-oriented service generally supports connection-related features such as sequencing, flow control and error control.
The Internet network layer is commonly described as connectionless/datagram based.

visualization.description: Would you build a road trip around independent GPS decisions or a pre-established route?

interactiveActivity.description: Toggle between datagram mode and virtual-circuit mode and watch packet paths.

quickCheck.question: Classify five scenarios as connectionless or connection-oriented.

practice.question: Arrange TCP establishment messages. Focus topic: Connectionless vs Connection-Oriented Networks.
A fast sender overwhelms a slow receiver. Is this flow control or congestion control? Apply it to: Connectionless vs Connection-Oriented Networks.
Network routers are overloaded and packets are being lost. Is this flow control or congestion control? Explain your choice using the concepts from Connectionless vs Connection-Oriented Networks.

quiz.question: Which service requires logical connection establishment?
quiz.explanation: A connection-oriented service establishes and terminates a logical connection.

quiz.question: In a connectionless service, packets are generally treated as what?
quiz.explanation: Datagrams are handled independently.

quiz.question: Which is associated with connection-oriented service?
quiz.explanation: Connection-oriented service includes setup, maintenance and termination.

modules.title: Routing Algorithms & Optimality Principle
learningObjectives: Explain why routing algorithms are needed.
Relate shortest paths to routing decisions.

lesson.hook: Why does routing algorithms & optimality principle matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Routing algorithms calculate paths through a network.
The optimality principle states that if router J lies on the optimal path from I to K, the optimal path from J to K is part of that path.
Routing information is used to construct forwarding decisions.
Routing can be centralized or decentralized depending on the algorithm.

visualization.description: If a route from A to C passes through B, what should the best B→C route look like?

interactiveActivity.description: Build a graph and let the learner test candidate paths; highlight the subpath property.

quickCheck.question: Find the least-cost path in a weighted router graph.

practice.question: Classify a dotted-decimal address as IPv4 or identify an IPv6 hexadecimal address. Focus topic: Routing Algorithms & Optimality Principle.
practice.answer: Dotted-decimal 32-bit form is IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal form is IPv6.

practice.question: For /27, calculate host bits and the standard usable-host count. Apply it to: Routing Algorithms & Optimality Principle.
practice.answer: 5 host bits; 2^5 − 2 = 30 usable hosts under the traditional subnet convention.

practice.question: A host knows a destination IP on its local network but not the MAC. What should it use? Explain your choice using the concepts from Routing Algorithms & Optimality Principle.

quiz.question: The optimality principle concerns what?
quiz.explanation: The principle states that optimal paths contain optimal subpaths.

quiz.question: A routing algorithm is used mainly to determine what?
quiz.explanation: Routing algorithms determine paths.

quiz.question: A shortest-path algorithm compares what?
quiz.explanation: Shortest-path routing minimizes an assigned path cost.

modules.title: Shortest Path Routing
learningObjectives: Apply shortest-path routing to a network graph.

lesson.hook: Why does shortest path routing matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Shortest-path routing selects a path with minimum total cost.
A network can be represented as nodes and weighted links.
The cost may represent a metric assigned to a link.
The shortest path becomes the basis for forwarding toward the destination.

visualization.description: Which route would a packet choose when three paths have costs 4, 7 and 10?

interactiveActivity.description: Interactive graph where students click edges to build the least-cost route.

quickCheck.question: Calculate the least-cost route between two specified nodes.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Shortest Path Routing.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Shortest Path Routing.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Shortest Path Routing.

quiz.question: If three routes cost 4, 7 and 10, which is shortest?
quiz.explanation: The route with the minimum cost is selected.

quiz.question: In shortest-path routing, a link weight represents what?
quiz.explanation: Weights represent costs used for path selection.

quiz.question: What does the selected shortest path help create?
quiz.explanation: The selected route contributes to forwarding decisions.

modules.title: Flooding, Broadcast & Multicast
learningObjectives: Analyze duplicate packet risks in flooding.

lesson.hook: Why does flooding, broadcast & multicast matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Flooding forwards a packet on multiple outgoing links, subject to controls used to limit duplicates.
Broadcast targets all relevant nodes in a network.
Multicast targets a selected group of receivers.
These delivery patterns differ from ordinary unicast delivery.

visualization.description: What happens if every router forwards a packet to every neighbor?

interactiveActivity.description: Animated flood with TTL/duplicate suppression controls; switch between unicast, broadcast and multicast.

quickCheck.question: Choose the delivery mode for three communication scenarios.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Flooding, Broadcast & Multicast.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Flooding, Broadcast & Multicast.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Flooding, Broadcast & Multicast.

quiz.question: Flooding forwards a packet over what?
quiz.explanation: Flooding forwards through multiple links.

quiz.question: Broadcast is intended for what audience?
quiz.explanation: Broadcast reaches all relevant receivers.

quiz.question: Multicast targets what?
quiz.explanation: Multicast is group-oriented delivery.

modules.title: Distance Vector Routing
learningObjectives: Update a routing-table entry using neighbor information.

lesson.hook: Why does distance vector routing matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Each router maintains distance information to destinations and exchanges information with directly connected neighbors.
A router can combine its cost to a neighbor with that neighbor's advertised distance.
Repeated exchanges allow routers to learn lower-cost paths.
The router also tracks the next hop used for a destination.

visualization.description: How can a router learn about a destination it cannot reach directly?

interactiveActivity.description: Animated neighbor updates showing routing-table convergence.

quickCheck.question: Perform one distance-vector update using a small table.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Distance Vector Routing.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Distance Vector Routing.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Distance Vector Routing.

quiz.question: Distance-vector routers exchange information primarily with whom?
quiz.explanation: Distance-vector routing exchanges information with directly connected neighbors.

quiz.question: A route via neighbor A can be evaluated using what?
options: Cost to A + A's advertised distance
quiz.explanation: Distance-vector updates combine local cost with neighbor distance.

quiz.question: What changes as distance-vector updates converge?
quiz.explanation: Repeated updates lead toward least-cost information.

modules.title: Count-to-Infinity Problem
learningObjectives: Describe why slow convergence is dangerous.

lesson.hook: Why does count-to-infinity problem matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Distance-vector routing can temporarily contain incorrect information after a route failure.
Routers may increase a metric repeatedly while believing a failed destination is reachable through one another.
This behavior is called count to infinity.
The problem illustrates the need for mechanisms that improve convergence.

visualization.description: Two routers keep telling each other that a failed destination is reachable. What goes wrong?

interactiveActivity.description: Failure simulation where route metrics increment over time.

quickCheck.question: Identify the routing failure pattern that represents count to infinity.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Count-to-Infinity Problem.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Count-to-Infinity Problem.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Count-to-Infinity Problem.

quiz.question: Count to infinity is associated with which routing family?
quiz.explanation: Count to infinity is a classic distance-vector problem.

quiz.question: What can trigger count to infinity?
options: A route failure with misleading neighbor information
quiz.explanation: Failures can cause routers to circulate incorrect reachability information.

quiz.question: The count-to-infinity problem mainly reflects what?
quiz.explanation: It is a convergence/loop problem.

modules.title: Link State Routing
learningObjectives: Compare global topology knowledge with neighbor-only distance knowledge.

lesson.hook: Why does link state routing matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Link-state routing distributes information about router neighbors/links through the network.
Routers build a view of network topology and use it to calculate routes.
The source material describes flooding of neighbor information.
Link-state routing is dynamic and supports topology-based path calculation.

visualization.description: What if every router knew the network map instead of only neighbor distances?

interactiveActivity.description: Topology map fills as link-state information is flooded.

quickCheck.question: Trace how a link-state update changes a router's topology database.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Link State Routing.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Link State Routing.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Link State Routing.

quiz.question: In link-state routing, routers share knowledge about what?
quiz.explanation: Routers advertise information about their links/neighbors.

quiz.question: How is link-state information distributed in the source material?
quiz.explanation: The material states that neighbor information is sent through flooding.

quiz.question: Link-state routing relies on what broad view?
quiz.explanation: Routers build topology information.

modules.title: Path Vector Routing & BGP Concept
learningObjectives: Understand why AS-level path information matters.
Relate path vectors to inter-domain routing.

lesson.hook: Why does path vector routing & bgp concept matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Path-vector routing carries path information rather than only a scalar distance.
The course material identifies path-vector routing as part of Network Layer routing.
Inter-domain routing must consider autonomous-system-level paths and policy.
BGP is the major Internet inter-domain routing protocol associated with path-vector routing.

visualization.description: How can a router avoid choosing a route that loops through an AS already in the path?

interactiveActivity.description: Animate AS path lists and highlight loop detection.

quickCheck.question: Inspect candidate AS paths and select a path that avoids an existing AS.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Path Vector Routing & BGP Concept.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Path Vector Routing & BGP Concept.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Path Vector Routing & BGP Concept.

quiz.question: Path-vector routing advertises what extra information?
quiz.explanation: Path-vector routing carries path information.

quiz.question: BGP is primarily associated with what type of routing?
quiz.explanation: BGP is the Internet's inter-domain routing protocol.

quiz.question: An AS path can help detect what?
quiz.explanation: Repeated AS entries can indicate a loop.

modules.title: Hierarchical Routing
learningObjectives: Explain why hierarchy is needed in large networks.

lesson.hook: Why does hierarchical routing matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: As a network grows, complete routing information becomes expensive to store and process.
Hierarchical routing divides routers into regions.
Routers maintain detailed information for their own region and summarized information for other regions.
This reduces routing-table size and improves scalability.

visualization.description: Why shouldn't every router store a detailed route to every router on the Internet?

interactiveActivity.description: Compare a flat routing table with a region-based table.

quickCheck.question: Choose the hierarchical route when the destination is in another region.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Hierarchical Routing.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Hierarchical Routing.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Hierarchical Routing.

quiz.question: Why is hierarchical routing useful?
quiz.explanation: Hierarchy summarizes information and improves scalability.

quiz.question: Routers in a region usually know detailed information about what?
quiz.explanation: Hierarchical routing keeps detailed local information.

quiz.question: What can hierarchical routing reduce?
quiz.explanation: Summarization reduces table size.

modules.title: Congestion Control Algorithms
learningObjectives: Identify retransmission/window policies as congestion-related mechanisms.

lesson.hook: Why does congestion control algorithms matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Congestion occurs when offered network load exceeds capacity and performance degrades.
Open-loop control aims to prevent congestion before it happens.
Closed-loop control reacts after congestion has occurred.
The source material discusses retransmission policy, window policy, acknowledgment policy, backpressure and choke-packet techniques.

visualization.description: Why can careless retransmission make congestion worse?

interactiveActivity.description: Traffic-load animation showing queues overflow as retransmissions increase.

quickCheck.question: Classify a congestion mechanism as preventive or reactive.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Congestion Control Algorithms.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Congestion Control Algorithms.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Congestion Control Algorithms.

quiz.question: Congestion occurs when load is greater than what?
quiz.explanation: The source defines congestion as load exceeding capacity.

quiz.question: Open-loop congestion control attempts to do what?
quiz.explanation: Open-loop methods are preventive.

quiz.question: Closed-loop congestion control reacts when?
quiz.explanation: Closed-loop control removes/reacts to existing congestion.

modules.title: Quality of Service (QoS)
learningObjectives: Identify delay, throughput and reliability-related requirements.

lesson.hook: Why does quality of service (qos) matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: QoS describes characteristics of the service delivered by a network.
Relevant requirements can include delay, throughput, loss/error levels, priority and resilience.
Different applications can prefer different QoS characteristics.
For example, a high-throughput transfer and a low-delay transaction may have different requirements.

visualization.description: Why might a video call care about delay more than a file download?

interactiveActivity.description: Adjust delay, throughput and loss sliders and observe application suitability.

quickCheck.question: Select the QoS parameter most important for a given application.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: Quality of Service (QoS).
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: Quality of Service (QoS).
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from Quality of Service (QoS).

quiz.question: Which is a QoS parameter?
quiz.explanation: Throughput is explicitly listed as a QoS parameter.

quiz.question: What does delay measure in this context?
options: Time taken between sending and receiving
quiz.explanation: Delay is the time between sending and receiving.

quiz.question: A high-throughput application primarily needs what?
quiz.explanation: Throughput measures data transferred per second.

modules.title: IP Addressing & Classful Addressing
learningObjectives: Identify network ID and host ID concepts.
Recognize Class A through Class E categories from the supplied material.

lesson.hook: Why does ip addressing & classful addressing matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: IP addresses are logical/software-based network addresses.
The supplied material describes IPv4 addresses as 32 bits in dotted-decimal notation.
Classful addressing divides IPv4 into Classes A, B, C, D and E.
Network ID identifies the network portion and Host ID identifies hosts within that network.

visualization.description: How does a router distinguish one network from another using an IP address?

interactiveActivity.description: Split a 32-bit IPv4 address into network and host portions.

quickCheck.question: Classify sample addresses using the class ranges provided in the course material.

practice.question: Classify a dotted-decimal address as IPv4 or identify an IPv6 hexadecimal address. Focus topic: IP Addressing & Classful Addressing.
practice.answer: Dotted-decimal 32-bit form is IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal form is IPv6.

practice.question: For /27, calculate host bits and the standard usable-host count. Apply it to: IP Addressing & Classful Addressing.
practice.answer: 5 host bits; 2^5 − 2 = 30 usable hosts under the traditional subnet convention.

practice.question: A host knows a destination IP on its local network but not the MAC. What should it use? Explain your choice using the concepts from IP Addressing & Classful Addressing.

quiz.question: An IPv4 address is how many bits long?
quiz.explanation: The source material states IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.

quiz.question: What does the Host ID represent?
quiz.explanation: Host ID represents hosts in the network.

quiz.question: Which set is the classful IPv4 classification listed in the material?
quiz.explanation: The material lists Classes A through E.

lesson.hook: Why does cidr & subnetting matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Subnetting divides a larger network into smaller subnetworks.
A subnet mask separates network/subnet bits from host bits.
CIDR uses prefix length notation such as /24 to indicate network-prefix length.
Usable-host calculations depend on the number of host bits and the addressing convention being used.

visualization.description: If a network is too large for one broadcast domain, how can it be divided?

interactiveActivity.description: Interactive bit-slider that changes prefix length and shows network/host portions.

quickCheck.question: Calculate the number of host bits and usable addresses for a prefix.

practice.question: Classify a dotted-decimal address as IPv4 or identify an IPv6 hexadecimal address. Focus topic: CIDR & Subnetting.
practice.answer: Dotted-decimal 32-bit form is IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal form is IPv6.

practice.question: For /27, calculate host bits and the standard usable-host count. Apply it to: CIDR & Subnetting.
practice.answer: 5 host bits; 2^5 − 2 = 30 usable hosts under the traditional subnet convention.

practice.question: A host knows a destination IP on its local network but not the MAC. What should it use? Explain your choice using the concepts from CIDR & Subnetting.

quiz.question: What does /24 indicate in CIDR?
quiz.explanation: CIDR prefix length specifies the number of network-prefix bits.

quiz.question: Subnetting is used to do what?
options: Divide a larger network into smaller subnetworks
quiz.explanation: Subnetting divides networks into smaller subnetworks.

quiz.question: For /27, how many host bits remain in IPv4?
quiz.explanation: 32 total bits minus 27 network bits leaves 5 host bits.

modules.title: Supernetting & VLSM
learningObjectives: Choose different subnet sizes for different requirements.

lesson.hook: Why does supernetting & vlsm matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Supernetting combines contiguous networks into a larger address block.
VLSM allows different subnet sizes within an addressing plan.
VLSM is useful when different network segments need different host capacities.
CIDR-style prefix lengths support flexible allocation.

visualization.description: Why waste a /24 on a link that needs only a few hosts?

interactiveActivity.description: Drag-and-drop VLSM blocks into departments with different host requirements.

quickCheck.question: Allocate suitable prefix sizes for three departments with different host counts.

practice.question: Classify a dotted-decimal address as IPv4 or identify an IPv6 hexadecimal address. Focus topic: Supernetting & VLSM.
practice.answer: Dotted-decimal 32-bit form is IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal form is IPv6.

practice.question: For /27, calculate host bits and the standard usable-host count. Apply it to: Supernetting & VLSM.
practice.answer: 5 host bits; 2^5 − 2 = 30 usable hosts under the traditional subnet convention.

practice.question: A host knows a destination IP on its local network but not the MAC. What should it use? Explain your choice using the concepts from Supernetting & VLSM.

quiz.question: VLSM stands for what?
quiz.explanation: VLSM means Variable Length Subnet Mask.

quiz.question: Why use VLSM?
options: To allocate subnet sizes according to different needs
To force all subnets to be equal
quiz.explanation: VLSM supports different subnet sizes.

quiz.question: Supernetting generally combines what?
quiz.explanation: Supernetting aggregates contiguous networks.

modules.title: IPv4 Protocol & Packet Format
learningObjectives: Understand packet fragmentation at a conceptual level.

lesson.hook: Why does ipv4 protocol & packet format matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: IPv4 provides IP addressing, host-to-host communication, packet formatting and fragmentation.
An IPv4 packet contains a header followed by payload.
Routers use destination addressing to determine forwarding.
Fragmentation can break a packet into smaller units when required by network constraints.

visualization.description: What information lets the network layer know where an IPv4 packet is going?

interactiveActivity.description: Click each IPv4 header field to reveal its purpose.

quickCheck.question: Match IPv4 header fields to their functions.

practice.question: Classify a dotted-decimal address as IPv4 or identify an IPv6 hexadecimal address. Focus topic: IPv4 Protocol & Packet Format.
practice.answer: Dotted-decimal 32-bit form is IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal form is IPv6.

practice.question: For /27, calculate host bits and the standard usable-host count. Apply it to: IPv4 Protocol & Packet Format.
practice.answer: 5 host bits; 2^5 − 2 = 30 usable hosts under the traditional subnet convention.

practice.question: A host knows a destination IP on its local network but not the MAC. What should it use? Explain your choice using the concepts from IPv4 Protocol & Packet Format.

quiz.question: Which address identifies the destination of an IPv4 packet?
quiz.explanation: The destination IP address identifies the target host/interface.

quiz.question: IPv4 supports what packet operation when necessary?
quiz.explanation: The source material identifies fragmentation as an IP responsibility.

quiz.question: IP is responsible for which communication scope?
quiz.explanation: The network layer provides host-to-host delivery.

modules.title: IPv6 Protocol & IPv4-to-IPv6 Transition
learningObjectives: Distinguish IPv4 and IPv6 address sizes.
Explain the need for transition mechanisms conceptually.

lesson.hook: Why does ipv6 protocol & ipv4-to-ipv6 transition matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.
IPv6 was designed to address the limitations of IPv4 address space and support continued Internet growth.
IPv4 and IPv6 use different address formats.
Transition requires mechanisms that allow IPv4 and IPv6 environments to coexist during migration.

visualization.description: What changes when an address grows from 32 bits to 128 bits?

interactiveActivity.description: Expand a compact IPv6 address into its hexadecimal groups and compare it with dotted-decimal IPv4.

quickCheck.question: Identify whether sample addresses are IPv4 or IPv6.

practice.question: Classify a dotted-decimal address as IPv4 or identify an IPv6 hexadecimal address. Focus topic: IPv6 Protocol & IPv4-to-IPv6 Transition.
practice.answer: Dotted-decimal 32-bit form is IPv4; colon-separated hexadecimal form is IPv6.

practice.question: For /27, calculate host bits and the standard usable-host count. Apply it to: IPv6 Protocol & IPv4-to-IPv6 Transition.
practice.answer: 5 host bits; 2^5 − 2 = 30 usable hosts under the traditional subnet convention.

practice.question: A host knows a destination IP on its local network but not the MAC. What should it use? Explain your choice using the concepts from IPv6 Protocol & IPv4-to-IPv6 Transition.

quiz.question: How many bits are in an IPv6 address?
quiz.explanation: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses.

quiz.question: IPv4 addresses are commonly written in what notation?
quiz.explanation: The source material describes IPv4 dotted-decimal notation.

quiz.question: Why are transition mechanisms needed?
options: IPv4 and IPv6 must coexist during migration
quiz.explanation: Transition supports coexistence while networks migrate.

modules.title: ARP, RARP & DHCP
learningObjectives: Explain ARP's role in local delivery.

lesson.hook: Why does arp, rarp & dhcp matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: ARP resolves a network-layer IP address to a data-link/MAC address on a local network.
RARP is the reverse direction concept: obtaining an IP address from a known hardware address.
DHCP provides hosts with IP configuration information dynamically.
The supplied material describes DHCP clients and servers and the DORA sequence in the broader course resources.

visualization.description: A host knows the destination IP but needs a local MAC address. What protocol helps?

interactiveActivity.description: Animate ARP request → ARP reply and DHCP Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge.

quickCheck.question: Choose ARP, RARP or DHCP for a described task.

modules.title: Transport Layer: Purpose & Services

It provides logical communication between application processes on different hosts.
Services include end-to-end delivery, addressing, reliable delivery, flow control and multiplexing.
Transport protocols operate in end systems rather than network routers.

modules.title: E-Mail Architecture & SMTP
learningObjectives: Describe email delivery between clients and mail servers.

lesson.hook: Why does e-mail architecture & smtp matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Email protocols govern transmission to and from mail servers.
SMTP is an application-layer protocol used for sending email.
The source material describes SMTP as connection-oriented and operating over TCP/IP.
Commands include MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA and QUIT.

visualization.description: When you press Send, does your mail client directly deliver the message to the recipient's inbox?

interactiveActivity.description: Animate sender client → sender mail server → recipient mail server.

quickCheck.question: Arrange the main SMTP conversation commands.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: E-Mail Architecture & SMTP.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: E-Mail Architecture & SMTP.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from E-Mail Architecture & SMTP.

quiz.question: SMTP is mainly used for what?
quiz.explanation: SMTP is used for email transfer.

quiz.question: Which SMTP command identifies the sender?
quiz.explanation: MAIL FROM identifies the sender.

quiz.question: Which command indicates that message data follows?
quiz.explanation: DATA signals the message body stream.

modules.title: POP3 & IMAP
learningObjectives: Compare download-oriented and server-maintained mailbox access.

lesson.hook: Why does pop3 & imap matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: POP3 is an application-layer email retrieval protocol.
The supplied material describes POP as supporting offline access and requiring download to access messages.
IMAP keeps messages on the remote server and allows mailbox manipulation there.
IMAP supports folders and searching and can support concurrent mailbox access.

visualization.description: Why can the same email appear consistently across phone and laptop with IMAP?

interactiveActivity.description: Compare a local-download POP model with server-side IMAP model.

quickCheck.question: Choose POP3 or IMAP for each mailbox scenario.

practice.question: Given link costs, select the minimum-total-cost route from source to destination. Focus topic: POP3 & IMAP.
practice.answer: Choose the path whose sum of link costs is smallest.

practice.question: A network grows very large. Which routing approach reduces per-router information by using regions? Apply it to: POP3 & IMAP.
Two routers repeatedly increase their metric for a failed destination. Identify the problem. Explain your choice using the concepts from POP3 & IMAP.

quiz.question: Which protocol keeps email on the remote server for manipulation?
quiz.explanation: The source material describes IMAP as server-maintained.

quiz.question: POP3 generally requires what to access messages?
quiz.explanation: The material says messages need to be downloaded for access.

quiz.question: Which protocol supports remote mailbox folders?
quiz.explanation: IMAP supports creating/manipulating remote message folders.

lesson.hook: Why does dns: domain name system matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: DNS is a client-server protocol used to translate names and IP addresses.
DNS uses a distributed database and hierarchical namespace.
The material describes root, TLD and authoritative servers.
Common records include A, AAAA, CNAME, MX and PTR.

visualization.description: How does a browser turn a human-readable domain name into an IP address?

interactiveActivity.description: Animate resolver → root → TLD → authoritative server → answer.

quickCheck.question: Identify the correct DNS record for IPv4, IPv6, alias and mail-server tasks.

practice.question: Trace a web request at a high level. Focus topic: DNS: Domain Name System.
practice.answer: Client/browser → DNS resolution → transport connection → HTTP request → HTTP response.

practice.question: Choose the protocol for name resolution, email sending, remote secure access and network management. Apply it to: DNS: Domain Name System.
practice.answer: DNS, SMTP, SSH and SNMP respectively.

practice.question: Choose POP3 or IMAP for a user who wants mail folders maintained on the server. Explain your choice using the concepts from DNS: Domain Name System.

quiz.question: Which record maps a name to an IPv4 address?
quiz.explanation: A records map hostnames to IPv4 addresses.

quiz.question: Which record maps a name to IPv6?
quiz.explanation: AAAA records map hostnames to IPv6 addresses.

quiz.question: DNS primarily uses which port in the course material?
quiz.explanation: The supplied material identifies UDP port 53 for DNS.

modules.title: Telnet
learningObjectives: Recognize its role as a remote terminal protocol.

lesson.hook: Why does telnet matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: Telnet provides remote terminal access over a network.
A Telnet client connects to a remote server process.
It is historically used for remote command-line interaction.
Because Telnet does not provide modern encrypted remote administration, it is mainly useful as a historical/application-layer concept in this course.

visualization.description: How could a user interact with a remote command-line system across a network?

interactiveActivity.description: Simulate a terminal session with client and server messages.

quickCheck.question: Identify whether a scenario represents remote terminal access.

practice.question: Trace a web request at a high level. Focus topic: Telnet.
practice.answer: Client/browser → DNS resolution → transport connection → HTTP request → HTTP response.

practice.question: Choose the protocol for name resolution, email sending, remote secure access and network management. Apply it to: Telnet.
practice.answer: DNS, SMTP, SSH and SNMP respectively.

practice.question: Choose POP3 or IMAP for a user who wants mail folders maintained on the server. Explain your choice using the concepts from Telnet.

quiz.question: Telnet is associated with what?
quiz.explanation: Telnet provides remote terminal-style access.

quiz.question: Telnet follows which broad interaction pattern?
quiz.explanation: A Telnet client connects to a remote server.

quiz.question: Telnet belongs to which layer?
quiz.explanation: Telnet is an application-layer protocol.

modules.title: SSH: Secure Remote Access
learningObjectives: Identify the SSH port given in the course material.

lesson.hook: Why does ssh: secure remote access matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: SSH provides secure remote access to systems.
It is used for encrypted remote administration and command-line sessions.
The supplied course material lists SSH on port 22.
SSH is an application-layer protocol that relies on lower-layer transport services.

visualization.description: What problem does secure remote administration solve compared with an unprotected terminal session?

interactiveActivity.description: Compare Telnet and SSH session paths; show encrypted payload for SSH.

quickCheck.question: Choose SSH when a scenario requires secure remote administration.

practice.question: Trace a web request at a high level. Focus topic: SSH: Secure Remote Access.
practice.answer: Client/browser → DNS resolution → transport connection → HTTP request → HTTP response.

practice.question: Choose the protocol for name resolution, email sending, remote secure access and network management. Apply it to: SSH: Secure Remote Access.
practice.answer: DNS, SMTP, SSH and SNMP respectively.

practice.question: Choose POP3 or IMAP for a user who wants mail folders maintained on the server. Explain your choice using the concepts from SSH: Secure Remote Access.

quiz.question: SSH is primarily used for what?
quiz.explanation: SSH provides secure remote access.

quiz.question: What port is listed for SSH in the course material?
quiz.explanation: The course material lists SSH as port 22.

quiz.question: SSH improves remote administration primarily through what?
quiz.explanation: SSH provides secure remote communication.

modules.title: SNMP, Streaming Media & RSA Overview
learningObjectives: Describe application-layer streaming at a high level.
Recognize RSA as a cryptographic algorithm included in the syllabus.

lesson.hook: Why does snmp, streaming media & rsa overview matter when real packets move across networks?
keyConcepts: SNMP is used to manage and monitor devices in IP networks.
The supplied material describes an SNMP manager controlling/monitoring agents such as routers.
Streaming audio/video delivers media progressively so playback can occur while data continues to arrive.
RSA is included in the supplied R18/R22-oriented Application Layer syllabus as a cryptographic algorithm topic.

visualization.description: How can an administrator monitor many routers without logging into each one manually?

interactiveActivity.description: Animate SNMP manager polling multiple network-device agents.

quickCheck.question: Match SNMP, streaming media and RSA to their high-level purpose.

practice.question: Trace a web request at a high level. Focus topic: SNMP, Streaming Media & RSA Overview.
practice.answer: Client/browser → DNS resolution → transport connection → HTTP request → HTTP response.

practice.question: Choose the protocol for name resolution, email sending, remote secure access and network management. Apply it to: SNMP, Streaming Media & RSA Overview.
practice.answer: DNS, SMTP, SSH and SNMP respectively.

practice.question: Choose POP3 or IMAP for a user who wants mail folders maintained on the server. Explain your choice using the concepts from SNMP, Streaming Media & RSA Overview.

quiz.question: SNMP is used primarily for what?
quiz.explanation: The source material defines SNMP as a network management protocol.

quiz.question: In SNMP, what controls/monitors agents?
quiz.explanation: The manager communicates with agents such as routers.

quiz.question: RSA in this course is categorized as what?
quiz.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes RSA under Unit V.
